questions.stem: Which list gives the EM spectrum bands in the order taught?

options.text: radio, gamma, infrared, x-ray, microwave, ultraviolet, visible
options.explanation: That shuffles the bands out of wavelength order.

options.text: gamma ray, x-ray, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwave, radio
options.explanation: The same seven bands, named from the shortest wavelength up.

options.text: radio, visible, microwave, infrared, gamma ray, x-ray, ultraviolet
options.explanation: That shuffles the middle bands.

options.text: microwave, radio, visible, infrared, x-ray, ultraviolet, gamma ray
options.explanation: Radio and microwave are swapped here.

questions.stem: In free space, all electromagnetic waves:

options.text: travel at speeds set by their frequency
options.explanation: Frequency changes across the spectrum; the speed does not.
EM waves are precisely the waves that need no medium.
Identical speed in a vacuum is the defining shared property.
All EM waves are transverse.

questions.stem: Which part of the EM spectrum does the human eye detect?

options.explanation: Those neighbours sit outside human detection.
Radio is far below the visible band in frequency.
Most of the spectrum is invisible to us.
Vision covers just the visible slice of the continuum.

questions.stem: The statement that the EM spectrum is continuous means:

options.text: the bands blend without gaps into one spectrum
options.explanation: Continuity means no missing stretches between the named bands.

options.text: all waves have the same wavelength
options.explanation: Wavelengths span an enormous range across the spectrum.
Continuity describes the spectrum, not motion.

options.text: each band is physically separated from the next
options.explanation: That is the opposite of continuity.

questions.stem: X-rays and radio waves both cross a vacuum. Compared with the radio waves, the x-rays travel:

options.text: faster, because their frequency is higher
options.explanation: Frequency does not change the vacuum speed.

options.text: slower, because their wavelength is shorter
options.explanation: Wavelength does not change the vacuum speed either.
Free space gives every EM wave the same speed.

options.text: at a speed that depends on the source
options.explanation: The shared free-space speed is source-independent.

questions.stem: State the three properties all EM waves share.
questions.modelAnswer: They are all transverse, they all pass through free space (a vacuum), and they all move at one shared speed through that vacuum.

questions.stem: Name the seven standard bands of the electromagnetic spectrum in order.
questions.modelAnswer: Gamma ray, x-ray, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwave and radio — the seven bands, shortest wavelength first.

questions.stem: Explain why astronauts on the Moon can see the Earth even though space is a vacuum.
questions.modelAnswer: Light is an electromagnetic wave, and EM waves travel through free space without needing particles, so the vacuum between Moon and Earth carries the light perfectly well.

questions.stem: A detector finds an EM wave of wavelength 5 x 10^-7 m, inside the visible band, and another of wavelength 500 m. State which band the long-wave signal occupies and one shared property of the two signals.
questions.modelAnswer: The 500 m signal is a radio wave; both signals move at one shared speed through free space (and both are transverse), whatever their wavelengths.

questions.stem: Which radiation has the longest wavelength in the EM spectrum?

options.explanation: Gamma is the short-wavelength end.
Radio sits at the long-wavelength, low-frequency end.
Ultraviolet sits just past visible, far from the long end.
Microwaves are second from the long end.

questions.stem: Across the EM spectrum, as wavelength decreases the frequency:

options.explanation: That would break the fixed wave speed.
Frequency spans a huge range across the spectrum.
No fixed doubling rule exists between bands.
Wavelength and frequency are inversely proportional.

questions.stem: Within the visible spectrum, the colour with the longest wavelength is:

options.explanation: Red is the long-wavelength, low-frequency end of the visible band.
Violet is the short-wavelength end.
Green sits mid-band.
Yellow is between green and red, not the extreme.

questions.stem: Gamma rays differ from radio waves by having:

options.explanation: That describes the radio end.

options.text: a higher speed in free space
options.explanation: All EM waves share one free-space speed.
Gamma is the short-and-fast extreme of the spectrum.
All EM waves are transverse.

questions.stem: An EM wave is found to have a higher frequency than violet light. Its wavelength compared with violet light is:

options.text: longer, to keep the speed constant
options.explanation: Longer wavelength would lower the frequency.
Frequency and wavelength cannot both match violet.
The inverse law gives the comparison directly.
Higher frequency forces shorter wavelength at fixed speed.

questions.stem: State the colour with the shortest wavelength in the visible spectrum.
questions.modelAnswer: Violet sits at the short-wavelength, high-frequency end of the visible colours.

questions.stem: State how frequency changes as you move from radio waves to gamma rays.
questions.modelAnswer: Frequency increases from radio waves to gamma rays as wavelength decreases.

questions.stem: Explain, using the wave equation, why the gamma-ray end of the spectrum has the highest frequencies.
questions.modelAnswer: All EM waves share one speed in free space through v = f x lambda, so the band with the shortest wavelength, gamma rays, must carry the highest frequency to keep the product constant.

questions.stem: A student lists visible colours from longest to shortest wavelength as violet, blue, green, yellow, orange, red. Correct the order and state the fixed property that makes only one order possible.
questions.modelAnswer: The correct order is red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet; only one order is possible because wavelength and frequency are inversely proportional at the fixed free-space speed, so each colour occupies a unique wavelength band.
